1.title: your grandmother before dinner
1.hook: your grandmother before dinner; a gift you didn't earn
1.howItsDone: Many Catholic families say a short grace before meals, often the traditional "Bless us, O Lord," and many make the sign of the cross before and after it.

segments.voice: Picture a kitchen table. The food is on it, steam coming off the potatoes, and somebody's already reaching for the bread. And then a hand on the wrist. Your grandmother, or someone's grandmother, saying: wait. Grace first. Heads go down. A few quick words, a quick amen, and then everybody eats. Millions of families have done this every night of their lives, and most kids at that table thought grace meant the little speech before dinner. It does. But the word is much bigger than the speech. It's the reason for the speech. Today's word is the first one on this path, and in a sense every other word sits on top of it.
screen: `A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `WAIT. GRACE FIRST.` → `THE WORD IS BIGGER THAN THE SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Grace comes from the Latin word gratia. It means a favor. A gift. Something given freely, not paid for. It's the same root that gives English the word gratitude, and the word gratis, meaning free of charge. The New Testament was written in Greek, and there the word is charis, which also means a gift freely given, and a kind of loveliness. So when Catholics talk about grace, they mean God's gift of himself, given before anybody earned it. The letter to the Ephesians says it plainly, in the old Douay-Rheims Bible that English-speaking Catholics used for centuries: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves. That's the surprise at the heart of the word. You don't climb up to grace. It comes down to you. Catholics say it arrives in many ways: in baptism, in the sacraments, in prayer, in an ordinary Tuesday when a friend calls at exactly the right moment. And here's where the dinner table comes back in. The old grace many Catholic families say goes like this: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Listen to what it notices. Thy gifts. Thy bounty. The food on the table is a small picture of the big thing. Somebody grew it, somebody cooked it, and before any of that, Catholics say, somebody gave the world to begin with. So saying grace isn't paying a fee before eating. It's noticing that you were given something. That's the whole shape of today's word: a gift you didn't earn, and the moment you notice it.
screen: `GRATIA — A FAVOR, A GIFT.` · `CHARIS — GIVEN FREELY.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES.` · `THE TABLE IS A SMALL PICTURE.` · then, large: `A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Before you breathe, think of one thing you have today that you didn't earn. The air, maybe. A person. A roof. Then breathe in slowly, all the way, and let it out. If you pray, you can say thank you with that breath. If you don't, just let yourself notice the gift.
Grace. A favor, a gift freely given. Catholics say it comes first, before anyone earns it. First word on your strand.
screen: `GRACE — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: you are already held. Grace means the gift came first. Today, before one meal, even a snack at your desk, pause for a single second and notice that it was given to you. That's day one. See you tomorrow.

2.title: the smallest prayer
2.hook: the smallest prayer; what the hand is tracing
2.carry: head, heart, shoulders — all of you
2.tomorrow: why people stand up when the book comes in
2.howItsDone: Catholics make the sign of the cross at the start and end of prayers and of the Mass, often after dipping their fingers in holy water on entering a church, touching forehead, chest, left shoulder and right shoulder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace: a gift you didn't earn, noticed at a kitchen table. Your line was: you are already held. Did you catch yourself noticing a gift? Day two.

You've seen it even if you've never done it. A soccer player jogging onto the field, touching forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. A grandmother passing a church on the bus. A pitcher before the first throw. Someone hearing bad news in a hospital hallway. It takes about two seconds, and nobody has to say a word out loud. It's so quick that people forget it's a prayer at all. It might be the smallest prayer there is, and it's how most Catholic prayers begin and end, including the grace from yesterday. Today, what the hand is actually tracing.
screen: `FOREHEAD, CHEST, SHOULDER, SHOULDER.` → `TWO SECONDS.` → `THE SMALLEST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: It's very old. Around the year 200, a Christian writer in North Africa named Tertullian described believers tracing a small cross on their foreheads all day long: when they got dressed, when they sat down to eat, when they lit a lamp. A tiny mark with a thumb. Over the centuries the small cross grew into the large one most Catholics make today. And the hand tells a story as it goes. It traces the cross, the shape Jesus died on, over your own body. At the same time, the words name who Catholics believe God is. They come from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends his friends out, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." So in two seconds you've said two big things: the cross, and the Trinity, one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Catholics say it's also a small reminder of their own baptism. That's why, walking into a church, many dip their fingers in holy water first, and then make the sign. Now look at where the hand goes. The forehead, where you think. The chest, where your heart is. Then both shoulders, where you carry things and do your work. Many Catholics hear it that way: the prayer covers all of you. Your thoughts, your feelings, your strength. A small detail you might notice at a friend's church: Catholics in the West usually go to the left shoulder first, then the right. Orthodox Christians go right, then left, and hold their fingers a particular way. Same sign, two old habits.
screen: `TERTULLIAN: A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD.` · `THE CROSS AND THE TRINITY.` · `A REMINDER OF BAPTISM.` · `THINK, FEEL, CARRY.` · then, large: `ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. One breath, with the bell. If you'd like to, make the sign of the cross slowly, slower than anyone ever does it: forehead, chest, left shoulder, right. If you'd rather not, just rest a hand on your forehead, then on your chest, then on each shoulder, and notice each place. Then one breath, all the way in and all the way out.
The sign of the cross. The cross traced over your own body, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Second word.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS — your 2nd word`.

segments.voice: Your line: head, heart, shoulders — all of you. Today, when you catch yourself thinking, feeling or carrying something heavy, notice which of the three it is. Day two.

screen: `DAY 2 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY PEOPLE STAND UP WHEN THE BOOK COMES IN.`

3.title: why people stand up when the book comes in
3.hook: why people stand up when the book comes in
3.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics sit for the first readings and the psalm, then stand for the Gospel, often tracing small crosses on the forehead, lips and heart as it is announced.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sign of the cross: forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. Your line was: head, heart, shoulders — all of you. Which one was carrying the most? Day three.

If you've ever been to a Catholic Mass as a guest, you know the feeling. Everyone else seems to know when to sit, when to stand, when to kneel, and you're half a second behind, watching the person in front of you. There's one moment that catches visitors most. People have been sitting quietly, listening to readings. Then music starts, often the word alleluia, and the whole room stands up at once. Someone at the front lifts a book up high. Why stand for a book? For the next three days we're going to walk through the Mass like a play in three scenes. Today, scene one: the story.
screen: `SIT, STAND, KNEEL.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `SCENE ONE: THE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Mass comes from the old Latin ending of the service, ite, missa est, roughly: go, you are sent. So the whole thing is named for the moment you walk back out the door. Now, scene one. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Word, and it's mostly listening. On a Sunday there's usually a reading from the Old Testament, then a psalm, often sung back and forth, then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles. People sit for those. Then comes the Gospel, one of the four books about the life of Jesus, and everyone stands. Gospel is an old English word, good news, for the Greek euangelion. Catholics say that when the Gospel is read, Christ himself is speaking to the people gathered there. So you stand the way you'd stand when someone important walks into the room. There's a small ritual right before it, too. Many people trace three little crosses with their thumb: on the forehead, on the lips, on the heart. Remember yesterday's sign? It's the same idea, shrunk down. The words be in my mind, on my lips, in my heart. Standing for the book isn't new, either. The Bible itself describes it. In the book of Nehemiah, after the exile, the scribe Ezra opens the book of the law in front of the whole people, and when he opens it, they all stand up. And in Luke's Gospel, when Jesus goes home to Nazareth, he goes to the synagogue and stands up to read the scroll of Isaiah. People have been rising for the reading for a very long time. Then everyone sits again, and a priest or deacon preaches: the homily. The story has entered the room, and scene one ends.
screen: `MASS — GO, YOU ARE SENT.` · `READINGS, A PSALM, THEN THE GOSPEL.` · `THREE SMALL CROSSES.` · `EZRA OPENS THE BOOK. THEY STAND.` · then, large: `THE STORY ENTERS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. If you're sitting, stand up, just for this, the way the room stands for the Gospel. On the first breath, touch your forehead. On the second, your lips. On the third, your heart. You don't have to say anything. Just let each place get ready to listen.
The Gospel. The good news: the reading about the life of Jesus that everyone stands to hear, the high point of scene one of the Mass. Third word.
Your line: the story enters the room. Today, when someone starts telling you something that matters to them, give it the full attention of a room standing up. Day three.

4.title: "peace be with you"
4.hook: "peace be with you" — the handshake in the middle
4.tomorrow: bread, wine, "do this in memory of me"
4.howItsDone: At Mass, after the Our Father and before communion, the priest invites the people to offer each other a sign of peace, and people turn to those nearby with a handshake, a bow or a nod, saying "peace be with you."

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gospel: the readings, and the whole room standing for the good news. Your line was: the story enters the room. Who did you really listen to? Day four.

Here's the moment first-time visitors remember. The Mass is quiet and formal. Candles, a priest at the altar, everyone facing forward, nobody talking. And then, out of nowhere, everyone turns around. The person behind you sticks out a hand. The teenager next to you, who hasn't looked up from the floor, says peace be with you. A couple kisses. A little kid waves at the whole row. For about thirty seconds, a room full of people who mostly don't know each other shakes hands. Then everyone turns back to the front as if nothing happened. Today, scene two of the Mass, and the handshake in the middle of it.
screen: `EVERYONE FACING FORWARD.` → `THEN EVERYONE TURNS AROUND.` → `THE HANDSHAKE IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: After the story comes the table. Catholics call the second half of the Mass the Liturgy of the Eucharist. Bread and wine are carried up to the altar, the priest prays over them, and the whole room says the Our Father together. Then, just before people come forward to receive communion, the sign of peace. Where does it come from? Start with Easter night. In John's Gospel, the frightened friends of Jesus are hiding behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. His first words, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Peace be to you." Not a scolding for running away. Peace. In the Greek, eirene, and behind it the Hebrew greeting shalom, which means more than quiet. It means whole, complete, nothing missing. The first Christians greeted each other with more than a handshake. Paul's letters tell them to greet one another with a holy kiss, and for centuries worship included what was called the kiss of peace. There's a reason it sits right before communion in the Catholic Mass. Jesus once said that if you're bringing a gift to the altar and remember that someone has something against you, leave the gift there, go and make peace first, then come back. So before people go up to the table, they turn to whoever's beside them. Not their best friend. Whoever happens to be there. It's short on purpose. It isn't a chat. It's a sign: before we go any further, we're at peace with each other. Some older Catholic rites put the gesture earlier in the Mass, and the words and the gesture vary from country to country: a bow, a nod, a handshake. The meaning holds: turn to the stranger.
screen: `AFTER THE STORY, THE TABLE.` · `PEACE BE TO YOU — EASTER NIGHT.` · `SHALOM — WHOLE, NOTHING MISSING.` · `MAKE PEACE, THEN COME TO THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. Think of three people. On the first breath, someone you love. On the second, someone you barely know: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who sold you coffee. On the third, someone you're not at peace with right now. With each breath out, picture turning to them and offering your hand. If you pray, you can wish each of them peace.
The sign of peace. Turning to whoever is beside you, just before the table, to say peace be with you. Fourth word.
Your line: turn to the stranger. Today, give one person you don't know a real greeting: a look in the eye, a hello, a small kindness. Day four.

5.title: bread, wine, "do this in memory of me"
5.hook: bread, wine, "do this in memory of me"
5.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest repeats the words of the Last Supper over bread and wine, and Catholics who are prepared come forward to receive communion, then are sent out with a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sign of peace: the room turning around to shake hands before going to the table. Your line was: turn to the stranger. Who did you greet? Day five.

Think of a meal your family makes on one day of the year. Somebody's stuffing. A soup nobody else gets right. When you eat it, you're not only eating. You're back at a table with people who might not be alive anymore. The taste carries the memory in. Now picture a room in Jerusalem, the night before Jesus died. A festival meal, the Passover, itself a meal of memory. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, hands it around, and says something nobody at that table had heard before. Today, the last scene of the Mass, and the words it's built on.
screen: `A MEAL THAT CARRIES PEOPLE BACK.` → `A ROOM IN JERUSALEM.` → `BREAD, BROKEN AND SHARED.`

segments.voice: Luke's Gospel tells it this way, in the Douay-Rheims Bible. Jesus takes the bread, and says: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Then the cup, which he calls the new covenant in his blood. At every Catholic Mass, the priest says those words again over bread and wine at the altar. It's the center of the whole service, the moment everything has been walking toward. Catholics call it the Eucharist, from the Greek eucharistia, thanksgiving, because before he broke the bread, Jesus gave thanks. Here's the word underneath commemoration. In Greek it's anamnesis. It doesn't mean remembering the way you remember a phone number. It means making something present by remembering it. The Passover already worked that way. At that meal, Jewish families told the story of leaving Egypt as if they themselves had walked out. Catholics say the Mass works like that, and more. They believe that at those words, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ, and that the one sacrifice of the cross is made present again, not repeated. That's a big claim, and we'll come back to it on day seventeen. Christians don't all agree about what happens. Orthodox Christians also speak of a real presence. Many Protestants understand the meal mainly as a memorial and a sign. What they all share is the table, and the command: do this. Then comes the ending. People come forward and receive communion, and the Mass closes with a blessing and a sending out. Go, you are sent. Remember day three? The name of the Mass is in that sending. The story, the peace, the table, and then the door.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `ANAMNESIS — MEMORY THAT MAKES PRESENT.` · `CHRISTIANS DON'T ALL AGREE.` · `THE TABLE, THEN THE DOOR.` · then, large: `A MEAL IS A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one meal that carries someone for you. A dish, a table, a person who made it. On the first breath, see the table. On the second, see who's there. On the third, taste it. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, just let them be present for a moment.
The Eucharist. Thanksgiving: bread and wine, the words of the Last Supper, and communion, at the center of every Mass. Fifth word.
Your line: a meal is a memory. Today, at one meal, think of who taught you to eat it, grow it or make it. Day five.

6.title: a young woman says yes
6.howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary as the Mother of God and ask for her prayers, especially in the Hail Mary and the rosary; the Annunciation, the angel's visit, is celebrated every year on March 25.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharist: bread, wine, and do this in memory of me. Your line was: a meal is a memory. Who came to the table with you? Day six.

Picture a young woman in a small village in Galilee. Nazareth: a few dozen families, stone houses, a well. She's engaged to a local builder. She's young; Luke doesn't give her age, though girls were often promised in marriage young then. An ordinary day. And then, Luke's Gospel says, an angel named Gabriel is standing in the room, telling her she's going to have a child, and that he'll be called the Son of the Most High. She isn't married yet. She knows exactly what the village will say. Today, the most famous yes in the Catholic story, and the girl who said it.
screen: `A VILLAGE IN GALILEE.` → `AN ANGEL IN THE ROOM.` → `SHE KNOWS WHAT THEY'LL SAY.`

segments.voice: Her name, in Hebrew, was Miriam, like the sister of Moses. We say Mary. And the first thing Gabriel says to her, after the greeting, is what angels in the Bible almost always say: "Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God." Grace. Your first word, back again. Then she does something people skip over. She asks a question. How can this be? She isn't passive. She wants to understand. The angel answers, and then she gives the reply that Catholics have treasured for two thousand years. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, the word for be it done is fiat, and Catholics still call her answer Mary's fiat. Her yes. Here's why it matters so much. Catholics say God didn't force anything on her. He asked, and waited, and the whole story of Jesus turns on a young woman saying yes. That's why Catholics honor her more than any other saint. They call her the Mother of God, because they believe her son is God. They ask for her prayers, the way you'd ask a friend or your own mother to pray for you. And one thing matters to get right: Catholics honor Mary, but they don't worship her. Worship, in Catholic teaching, belongs to God alone. Other Christians differ on how much to say about her. Many Protestants honor her as a faithful believer and a model of trust, and don't pray to her. But nearly everyone who reads Luke sees the same courage: a girl, a question, and then yes.
screen: `MIRIAM — FEAR NOT.` · `SHE ASKS A QUESTION.` · `FIAT — BE IT DONE.` · `HONORED, NOT WORSHIPPED.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THE HANDMAID OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one thing in your life right now that you're resisting. Something you can't change and keep pushing against. On the first breath, name it. On the second, notice how tight you're holding it. On the third, breathe out, and let your hands open a little. If you pray, you can borrow Mary's words: be it done to me.
Mary. Miriam of Nazareth, the mother of Jesus, whose yes, her fiat, Catholics honor above every other saint. Sixth word.
Your line: let it be. Today, when something doesn't go your way, try asking one honest question about it first, the way she did, and then see if you can let it be. Day six.

7.title: not statues
7.hook: not statues — people with terrible flaws who kept going
7.tomorrow: the rich kid who gave his clothes back
7.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate saints' feast days through the year and on All Saints' Day, November 1; many are named for a saint and ask the saints, especially their patron saint, to pray for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary: a young woman, a question, and a yes. Your line was: let it be. And that's a week. Grace, the sign of the cross, the Gospel, the sign of peace, the Eucharist, Mary. Day seven.

Walk into an old Catholic church and you'll see them everywhere. Plaster figures in niches. Faces in stained glass. A man holding keys, a woman holding a wheel, a guy with a lamb. They look calm and a little unreal, like people who never had a bad day in their lives. That's the picture most people carry of a saint: someone born good, floating above it all. Catholics would tell you that picture is almost exactly wrong. The man holding the keys once swore three times that he'd never met his best friend. Today's word: not statues, people.
screen: `FACES IN STAINED GLASS.` → `THEY LOOK UNREAL.` → `NOT STATUES. PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Saint comes from the Latin sanctus, holy. In the New Testament, Paul writes letters to the saints in Rome and Corinth, and he means ordinary believers, people with jobs and arguments and debts. Later, the word came to mean especially the people the Church believes are now with God in heaven, and holds up as examples. So take the man with the keys. That's Peter. On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter was asked three times whether he knew him, and three times he said no. Then a rooster crowed, and the Gospels say he went out and wept bitterly. That's the first leader of the apostles, the one Catholics count as the first pope. Or take Augustine, one of the greatest thinkers the Church ever had. In his Confessions he admits that as a young man he prayed, more or less, make me pure, but not yet. Or Paul himself, who spent his early years hunting down Christians. The saints aren't people who never fell. They're people who fell and kept getting up. Here's the part Catholics love. They believe in what the old creed calls the communion of saints: that the living and the dead who belong to Christ are one family, and the family can still pray for each other. So a Catholic might ask a saint to pray for them the way you'd ask a grandmother. The statues are something like family photos on the wall. Nobody prays to the plaster. It's a reminder of who else is in the room. Other Christians see it differently: many Protestants honor the saints as examples and don't ask them for prayers. But the stories are the same stories. Flawed people, still going.
